text:
**Let the Market Park the Car: Why Cities Should Scrap Parking Minimums**

Somewhere in your city there's a vacant lot that should hold an apartment building, a bakery or a small clinic. Often the reason it's still empty has nothing to do with demand, money or neighborhood opposition. It's a line in the zoning code saying that every new home needs one and a half parking spaces, and every 1,000 square feet of retail needs four. The project doesn't pencil out once the asphalt is added, so nothing gets built.

Minimum parking requirements are one of the most expensive rules in city planning, and one of the least examined. Cities should get rid of them.

Start with what the rules actually do. A parking minimum doesn't create parking demand, and it doesn't manage it. It forces every builder to supply a fixed amount of parking whether or not the people who will live or work there need it. Planners usually set the numbers by looking at suburban sites at peak hours, where parking was free and nearly everyone drove. Then they apply those numbers to every block in the city. Donald Shoup, the UCLA economist who has spent decades on this subject, calls the result a "pseudo-science": precise-looking figures with little behind them.

The costs are real, even though nobody sees a bill. A space in a structured or underground garage commonly costs tens of thousands of dollars to build, and in expensive cities it can cost far more. That money doesn't disappear. It goes into rents, home prices, the cost of groceries and the price of a restaurant meal. People who don't own a car pay for parking they will never use. These are disproportionately lower-income households, older residents and young people, so the rule works as a quiet transfer from people who don't drive to people who do.

Land is the second cost. Surface lots are the most common way to meet a minimum because they're the cheapest, and they eat up a lot of ground. In many American downtowns, a striking share of the land is given over to storing cars. Every acre of parking is an acre that isn't housing, jobs or tax revenue. It also pushes buildings apart, which makes walking less pleasant and transit less viable, which in turn makes people more dependent on cars. The rule creates the very demand it claims to serve.

The third cost is what never gets built. Minimums hit small and unusual projects hardest: the corner shop, the converted warehouse, the triplex on a narrow lot, the restaurant moving into an old storefront that has no room for a lot. Large developers can sometimes absorb the expense or negotiate a variance. Small builders and first-time entrepreneurs usually can't. A city that says it wants affordable housing and local business while keeping these rules is working against itself.

Repeal isn't hypothetical anymore. Buffalo dropped its citywide minimums in 2017. Minneapolis followed in 2021, and Austin, San Jose and others have done the same since. California barred minimums near major transit stops in 2022. Auckland, New Zealand, removed them across much of the city in 2016. The results have been undramatic in the best way. Developers still build parking, but they build the amount they think tenants and customers will pay for, which is often less than the old code required and sometimes about the same. Studies of Buffalo and Auckland found new projects providing fewer spaces than the old rules would have required, and more homes getting built. Nothing collapsed.

The usual objection is spillover: if new buildings come with less parking, residents will fill the street and neighbors will suffer. That worry is legitimate, but the answer is to manage the curb, not to mandate garages. Residential permit programs, meters priced to keep a few spaces open on each block, and time limits all deal with spillover directly. They also cost far less than requiring every building to carry an oversupply forever. Cities already know how to manage street parking. They just haven't been asked to.

Another objection is that some places really do need parking: a suburban big-box store, a stadium, a hospital. Repeal doesn't stop anyone from building parking. It stops the government from requiring a fixed amount. A grocery store with a regional customer base will still build a lot, because its business depends on one. The difference is that the decision rests with the people who pay for it and live with the consequences, not with a decades-old table in the zoning code.

Abolishing minimums won't fix housing costs, traffic or climate emissions by itself. It is, however, one of the rare reforms that costs a city almost nothing, requires no new spending and removes a barrier rather than adding one. It makes room for the small, ordinary buildings that make neighborhoods work. And it treats parking like other things people want: something you can buy, rather than something everyone has to pay for.

Cities have spent seventy years building for cars by decree. It's time to let them decide what to build for.
